title: Does the product of two permutations fix a point?
W: Alice holds a permutation π and Bob holds a permutation σ of n items. They want to know whether π after σ leaves some item where it was. A three-item gadget turns set disjointness into this problem, so about n bits are needed. Is about n bits always enough, or do they really need n log n?
M: Let $\mathrm{FIX}_n(\pi,\sigma)=1$ iff there is $i\in[n]$ with $\pi(\sigma(i))=i$. On each block of three points, Alice using $c$ if her bit is 1 and $\mathrm{id}$ if it is 0, and Bob using $c^{-1}$ if his bit is 1 and $c$ if it is 0, where $c$ is a 3-cycle (so the block contains a fixed point of $\pi\sigma$ exactly when both bits are 1), embeds disjointness, giving $R(\mathrm{FIX}_n)=\Omega(n)$, while $R(\mathrm{FIX}_n)=O(n\log n)$ is trivial. Determine whether $R(\mathrm{FIX}_n)=\Theta(n)$, where $R$ is public-coin randomized communication complexity with error $1/3$.

title: Erdős–Szekeres by comparisons
W: Any list of k² + 1 distinct numbers contains k + 1 numbers that rise or fall in order. How many comparisons between entries does it take to actually find such a run? Patience sorting uses about N log k comparisons for a list of N = k² + 1 numbers. Can it be done with a constant number of comparisons per entry?
M: Let $N=k^2+1$ and let $T(k)$ be the least worst-case number of comparisons $a_i\overset{?}{<}a_j$ needed by a deterministic algorithm that, given distinct reals $a_1,\dots,a_N$, outputs indices $i_1<\dots<i_{k+1}$ with $(a_{i_t})$ monotone. Patience sorting gives $T(k)=O(N\log k)$. Decide whether $T(k)=O(N)$ or $T(k)=\Theta(N\log k)$. Also determine the randomized (expected-comparison) complexity.

title: Distances in four-peg Hanoi
W: In Tower of Hanoi with four pegs, the fewest moves between the two "all discs on one peg" positions is now known (Bousch, 2014). Give a polynomial-time method to find the fewest moves between any two legal positions, or show none exists under standard assumptions.
M: Let $H^4_n$ be the state graph of the Tower of Hanoi with 4 pegs and $n$ discs: vertices are $\{1,2,3,4\}^n$ (peg of each disc), and edges are legal single-disc moves. Is there an algorithm computing $d_{H^4_n}(u,v)$ for arbitrary $u,v\in\{1,2,3,4\}^n$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)$? (For 3 pegs this is linear time; for 4 pegs no subexponential algorithm is known to the author.)

title: Smallest zero-one multiple
W: Every n has a multiple written only with the digits 0 and 1, with at most n digits. Can the shortest such multiple be found in time polynomial in the number of digits of n? Or is deciding whether one exists with at most d digits NP-hard?
M: For $n\ge1$ coprime to 10 let $L(n)$ be the least number of digits of a positive multiple of $n$ whose decimal digits lie in $\{0,1\}$, i.e. the least $d$ with $\sum_{i\in S}10^i\equiv0\pmod n$ for some nonempty $S\subseteq\{0,\dots,d-1\}$. Decide whether the language $\{(n,1^d):L(n)\le d\}$ ($n$ in binary) is NP-hard under randomized polynomial-time reductions, or whether $L(n)$ can be computed in time $\mathrm{poly}(\log n)$.

title: Finding Huang's vertex
W: Huang's theorem says any set of more than half the corners of an n-dimensional cube contains a corner with at least √n neighbours in the set. When the set is given by a small circuit, how hard is it to find such a corner? Place this search problem among the known classes of total search problems.
M: $\mathrm{HUANG}$: given a Boolean circuit $f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}^n$ whose domain is read as $[2^{n-1}+1]$ (inputs beyond $2^{n-1}+1$ are ignored), output either $i\ne j$ with $f(i)=f(j)$, or indices $i,j_1,\dots,j_m$ with $m=\lceil\sqrt n\rceil$ such that $f(j_1),\dots,f(j_m)$ are distinct and each is at Hamming distance 1 from $f(i)$. By Huang's theorem and the pigeonhole principle this is a TFNP problem. Is $\mathrm{HUANG}\in\mathrm{FP}$? Is it in $\mathrm{PPP}$, $\mathrm{PPA}$ or $\mathrm{PLS}$, and is it complete for any standard subclass of TFNP?

title: The Mandelbrot set at Gaussian rationals
W: Is there an algorithm that takes a complex number with rational real and imaginary parts and decides whether it lies in the Mandelbrot set? Escaping points can be confirmed and attracting cycles can be found. But some Gaussian rationals, such as c = (37 + 16i)/100, lie on the boundary with an irrationally rotating fixed point, and other kinds of boundary point might hide there too.
M: Let $M=\{c\in\mathbb C:\ (f_c^{n}(0))_{n\ge0}\text{ bounded}\}$, $f_c(z)=z^2+c$. Prove or disprove that $M\cap\mathbb Q(i)$ is a decidable subset of $\mathbb Q(i)$. (The parameter $c=\mu/2-\mu^2/4$ with $\mu=(3+4i)/5$ equals $(37+16i)/100\in\partial M$; its fixed point has multiplier $\mu$, which is not a root of unity. Every element of $\mathbb Q(i)\setminus\mathbb Z[i]$ is neither a centre nor a Misiurewicz parameter, since those are algebraic integers.)

title: Recamán's sequence, faster
W: Recamán's sequence starts at 0 and at step n goes back by n if that lands on a new positive number, and otherwise goes forward by n. Computing the n-th term seems to need simulating all earlier steps. Is there an algorithm using substantially fewer than n steps?
M: Let $a_0=0$ and $a_n=a_{n-1}-n$ if $a_{n-1}-n>0$ and $a_{n-1}-n\notin\{a_0,\dots,a_{n-1}\}$, otherwise $a_n=a_{n-1}+n$. Is there an algorithm that computes $a_n$ (on a word-RAM with $O(\log n)$-bit words) in time $O(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ for some fixed $\varepsilon>0$? Or show that, for some natural model, $\Omega(n^{1-o(1)})$ time is necessary.

title: Integer complexity is NP-hard
W: The integer complexity of n is the fewest 1s needed to write n using +, × and brackets. Deciding whether it is at most k is in NP, since a short formula is a certificate. Is the problem NP-hard for n written in binary, or can it be solved in time polynomial in the number of digits?
M: Let $\|n\|$ be the least number of $1$'s in an expression for $n$ built from $1$, $+$, $\times$ and parentheses. Since $\|n\|\le3\log_2 n+O(1)$, the language $\{(n,k):\|n\|\le k\}$ with $n$ in binary lies in NP. Prove that it is NP-hard (possibly under randomized reductions), or show that $\|n\|$ can be computed in time $(\log n)^{O(1)}$.

title: Proof complexity of Graham–Pollak
W: The edges of a complete graph on n vertices cannot be split into fewer than n − 1 complete bipartite pieces. The known proofs use linear algebra. Written as a propositional formula, does this fact have short proofs in resolution, in cutting planes, or in low-degree sum-of-squares?
M: Let $\mathrm{GP}_n$ be the CNF with variables $\ell_{t,v},r_{t,v}$ ($t\in[n-2]$, $v\in[n]$) and auxiliary variables $e_{t,uv}\leftrightarrow(\ell_{t,u}\wedge r_{t,v})\vee(r_{t,u}\wedge\ell_{t,v})$, with clauses $\neg\ell_{t,v}\vee\neg r_{t,v}$, and for each edge $uv$ of $K_n$ the clauses saying exactly one $e_{t,uv}$ is true. $\mathrm{GP}_n$ is unsatisfiable by the Graham–Pollak theorem and has size $\mathrm{poly}(n)$. Determine whether $\mathrm{GP}_n$ has (a) resolution refutations of size $2^{n^{o(1)}}$, (b) polynomial-size cutting-planes refutations, (c) sum-of-squares refutations of degree $O(1)$.

title: Three Hadamard rows
W: There are no three ±1 rows of length n, with n twice an odd number, that are pairwise orthogonal. The reason is a short counting argument modulo 4. Encode this as a propositional formula. Do resolution or cutting planes need exponentially long proofs of it?
M: For $n\equiv2\pmod4$ let $\mathrm{HAD3}_n$ be the CNF on variables $x_{r,j}$ ($r\in\{1,2,3\}$, $j\in[n]$) with auxiliary variables $z_{rs,j}\leftrightarrow x_{r,j}\oplus x_{s,j}$ and sequential-counter clauses asserting $\sum_j z_{rs,j}=n/2$ for each pair $r<s$. It is unsatisfiable for all $n\equiv2\pmod4$ (checked by brute force for $n=2,6,10$, and satisfiable for $n=4,8$). Prove that resolution refutations of $\mathrm{HAD3}_n$ require size $2^{n^{\Omega(1)}}$, and determine whether cutting-planes refutations of size $n^{O(1)}$ (or $n^{O(\log n)}$) exist.

title: Highways of generalized Langton ants
W: A generalized Langton ant on a grid with k colours turns left or right according to a fixed rule word, steps the cell's colour forward, and moves on. Starting on a blank grid, some rules build a periodic "highway", some grow symmetric blobs forever, and some look chaotic. Show that no algorithm can tell, from the rule word, whether a highway eventually appears.
M: For $w\in\{L,R\}^k$ ($k\ge2$) the ant on $\mathbb Z^2$ starts at the origin facing north with all cells coloured $0$. At each step, on a cell of colour $c$ it turns by $w_c$, sets the colour to $c+1\bmod k$, and moves one cell forward. Say $w$ builds a highway if there are $t_0$, $p>0$ and $v\ne0$ such that for all $t\ge t_0$ the position at time $t+p$ is the position at time $t$ plus $v$, the heading at time $t+p$ equals the heading at time $t$, and the colours seen at times $t+p$ and $t$ agree. Prove that $\{w:\ w\text{ builds a highway}\}$ is undecidable, or show it is decidable.

title: Logic of random Latin squares
W: Pick a Latin square of order n uniformly at random and view it as a multiplication table on n symbols. Does every first-order statement about it have a limiting probability as n grows? A full zero-one law should fail. For example, the chance that some x satisfies x·x = x presumably tends to 1 − 1/e.
M: Let $L_n$ be a uniformly random Latin square on $[n]$, viewed as the structure $([n],\circ)$ with $x\circ y=L_n(x,y)$. Prove or disprove the first-order convergence law: for every first-order sentence $\varphi$ in the language $\{\circ\}$, $\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr[L_n\models\varphi]$ exists. As a first step, prove that $\Pr[\exists x\ (x\circ x=x)]\to1-e^{-1}$.

title: Finding a large convex polygon fast
W: Suk proved that among about 2^k points in general position in the plane there are always k forming a convex polygon. The classical cups-and-caps argument finds such a polygon quickly but needs about 4^k points. Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that finds a convex polygon as large as Suk's theorem promises?
M: Given $n$ points in general position in $\mathbb R^2$ (integer coordinates), output the vertices of a convex polygon formed by $k$ of them. Is there a deterministic (or randomized) algorithm running in time $n^{O(1)}$ that always succeeds with $k\ge(1-o(1))\log_2 n$? The Erdős–Szekeres cups-and-caps argument gives $k\ge(\tfrac12-o(1))\log_2 n$ in polynomial time, and Suk's theorem guarantees existence for $k=(1-o(1))\log_2 n$. Improving $\tfrac12$ to any constant $c>\tfrac12$ would already be of interest.

title: Rank of 3 × 3 by 3 × n matrix multiplication
W: Multiplying a 3 × 3 matrix by a 3 × n matrix takes some number of essential multiplications, which grows linearly in n. Find the exact growth constant. The tensor-rank lower bounds known for small cases do not settle it.
M: Let $R_n$ be the tensor rank over $\mathbb C$ of the matrix multiplication tensor $\langle3,3,n\rangle$. Since $R_{m+n}\le R_m+R_n$, the limit $\rho=\lim_{n\to\infty}R_n/n=\inf_n R_n/n$ exists, and $\rho\le R(\langle3,3,3\rangle)/3\le23/3$. Determine $\rho$. In particular, decide whether $\rho<23/3$.

title: Orbits of integer polynomial maps in the plane
W: Given a polynomial map of the plane with integer coefficients and two integer points, does iterating the map from the first point ever reach the second? For linear maps this is decidable (Kannan–Lipton), and in one variable it is easy. What about polynomial maps of two variables?
M: Is the following problem decidable: given $F=(F_1,F_2)\in\mathbb Z[x,y]^2$ and $a,b\in\mathbb Z^2$, decide whether $F^{(n)}(a)=b$ for some $n\ge0$? Also: is it decidable whether the orbit $\{F^{(n)}(a)\}$ is finite?

title: Integers with a predicate for sums of two squares
W: Take the integers with addition and a predicate saying "this number is a sum of two squares". Is the first-order theory of this structure decidable? Or does the predicate let one define multiplication? The analogous question for squarefree numbers has been settled positively.
M: Let $E=\{a^2+b^2:a,b\in\mathbb Z\}$. Is $\mathrm{Th}(\mathbb Z,+,0,1,E)$ decidable? Is $\mathrm{Th}(\mathbb Z,+,<,E)$ decidable? Determine whether multiplication on $\mathbb N$ is definable in $(\mathbb Z,+,<,E)$. (One expects decidability to hinge on asymptotics for patterns $\{n+h_i\in E,\ n+h'_j\notin E\}$.)

title: Closed sets whose sumset is the line
W: Among closed subsets F of the real line, consider those with F + F equal to the whole line. Find the exact descriptive complexity of this family. It is coanalytic by its definition; is it a complete coanalytic set, or is it Borel?
M: Let $\mathcal F(\mathbb R)$ carry the Effros Borel structure and let $\mathcal A=\{F\in\mathcal F(\mathbb R):F+F=\mathbb R\}$. Since $F+F=\bigcup_n(F_n+F_n)$ with $F_n=F\cap[-n,n]$ compact, $\mathcal A$ is $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_1$. Is $\mathcal A$ $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_1$-complete? The same question for $\{K\in\mathcal K([0,1]):K+K+K=[0,3]\}$ and for $\{F: F+F\supseteq[0,1]\}$.

title: Positive measure of rational self-similar sets
W: Shrink the line by rational factors and shift by rational amounts, several times over, and take the resulting self-similar fractal. Can a computer decide whether it has positive length? Positive length without interior is known to happen for some parameters, so testing for an interval is not obviously enough.
M: Given $k$ and rationals $r_1,\dots,r_k\in(0,1)$, $t_1,\dots,t_k$, let $K$ be the attractor of $\{x\mapsto r_ix+t_i\}$. Is $\{(r,t): \lambda(K)>0\}$ decidable? Is $\{(r,t):\mathrm{int}\,K\ne\emptyset\}$ decidable? Do they coincide for rational data?

title: Counting transversals of the cyclic Latin square
W: The addition table of the integers mod n is a Latin square. For odd n its transversals (one cell per row and column with all symbols different) number roughly e^{-1/2} (n!)²/n^{n-1}, and exact counts are known only for small n. Show that computing the exact count is as hard as every counting problem with unary input, or find a polynomial-time method.
M: For odd $n$ let $T(n)$ be the number of permutations $\sigma\in S_n$ such that $i\mapsto i+\sigma(i)\bmod n$ is also a permutation. Prove that $n\mapsto T(n)$ (with $n$ in unary) is $\#\mathrm P_1$-complete under polynomial-time Turing reductions, or give an algorithm computing $T(n)$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)$.

title: Two Beatty sequences, existentially
W: Presburger arithmetic stays decidable when one adds the map n ↦ ⌊n√2⌋. With both ⌊n√2⌋ and ⌊n√3⌋ the full theory is expected to be undecidable. Is the purely existential part decidable? It amounts to solving systems of linear inequalities in which both floors appear.
M: Let $f(n)=\lfloor n\sqrt2\rfloor$ and $g(n)=\lfloor n\sqrt3\rfloor$. Is the existential theory of $(\mathbb Z,+,<,0,1,f,g)$ decidable? Equivalently: is there an algorithm that decides solvability in $\mathbb Z$ of finite systems of linear equations and inequalities in variables $x_i$ and terms $f(t),g(t)$, with $t$ ranging over such terms (nesting allowed)?

title: Dimension of the critical almost Mathieu spectrum
W: The critical almost Mathieu operator has a Cantor-set spectrum whose fractal dimension depends delicately on the frequency α. Is this dimension a computable function of α? That is, given a program that computes α, can one compute the dimension to any accuracy?
M: For irrational $\alpha$ let $\Sigma_\alpha$ be the spectrum of $(H_{\alpha}u)(n)=u(n+1)+u(n-1)+2\cos(2\pi n\alpha)u(n)$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb Z)$, and let $d(\alpha)=\dim_H\Sigma_\alpha$ (known to satisfy $d(\alpha)\le1/2$). Is there an algorithm that, given an oracle for the binary digits of an irrational $\alpha$ and $n\in\mathbb N$, outputs a rational within $2^{-n}$ of $d(\alpha)$? If not uniformly, is $d(\alpha)$ at least a computable real for every computable irrational $\alpha$?

title: Colouring Mycielski graphs in resolution
W: The Mycielski graphs are triangle-free graphs whose chromatic number goes up by one at each step. They are notoriously hard colouring benchmarks for SAT solvers. Does resolution need exponentially long proofs that the k-th one cannot be coloured with k − 1 colours, measured against the size of the graph?
M: Let $M_2=K_2$ and $M_{k+1}=\mu(M_k)$ (Mycielski construction), so $|V(M_k)|=3\cdot2^{k-2}-1$ and $\chi(M_k)=k$. Let $\mathrm{COL}(M_k,k-1)$ be the standard CNF asserting a proper $(k-1)$-colouring. Does $\mathrm{COL}(M_k,k-1)$ have resolution refutations of size $|V(M_k)|^{O(1)}$? Or is size $2^{|V(M_k)|^{\Omega(1)}}$ necessary?

title: Polynomial-time digits of the percolation threshold
W: The critical probability for site percolation on the square grid, about 0.5927, can be computed to any accuracy using finite-box criteria, but the known methods take time exponential in the number of digits. Is there an algorithm producing n correct binary digits in time polynomial in n?
M: Let $p_c=p_c^{\mathrm{site}}(\mathbb Z^2)$. Is $p_c$ polynomial-time computable, i.e., is there an algorithm that on input $1^n$ outputs a dyadic rational $q$ with $|q-p_c|\le2^{-n}$ in time $n^{O(1)}$?

title: Parity of the partition function, fast
W: The number of partitions p(n) has about √n digits and can be computed in about √n time. Its parity is a single bit. Can the parity be computed substantially faster than p(n) itself?
M: Is there an algorithm that computes $p(n)\bmod 2$ in time $O(n^{1/2-\delta})$ for some fixed $\delta>0$ (bit operations, $n$ given in binary)? Is there one running in time $n^{o(1)}$?

title: Polynomial-time entropy of the logistic family
W: The topological entropy of the logistic map x ↦ ax(1 − x) is a continuous function of a that can be computed from the kneading sequence. But the known error bounds force exponentially long kneading data for n correct digits. Is the entropy polynomial-time computable at rational a?
M: Let $h(a)$ be the topological entropy of $x\mapsto ax(1-x)$ on $[0,1]$, $a\in[1,4]$. Is there an algorithm that, given rational $a$ and $n$, outputs a rational within $2^{-n}$ of $h(a)$ in time polynomial in $n$ and the bit size of $a$?

title: Counting squarefree numbers faster
W: How quickly can one count exactly the squarefree numbers up to x? Known methods take time around x^{2/5}. Is there an algorithm using about the cube root of x, or less?
M: Let $Q(x)=\#\{n\le x: n\text{ squarefree}\}=\sum_{d\le\sqrt x}\mu(d)\lfloor x/d^2\rfloor$. Is there an algorithm computing $Q(x)$ exactly in time $x^{1/3+o(1)}$? Is there one running in time $x^{\varepsilon}$ for every $\varepsilon>0$?

title: Word equations with square-free unknowns
W: Solving equations between words with unknown pieces is decidable (Makanin), even with regular constraints on the unknowns. What if some unknowns must be square-free, meaning they contain no block repeated twice in a row? Square-freeness is not a regular property.
M: Let $A=\{a,b,c\}$ and let $\mathrm{SF}\subseteq A^*$ be the set of square-free words. Is the existential first-order theory of $(A^*,\cdot,a,b,c,\mathrm{SF})$ decidable? Equivalently: given a finite system of word equations with constants together with constraints $x_i\in\mathrm{SF}$ or $x_i\notin\mathrm{SF}$, can one decide whether it has a solution?

title: Shortest relation between two permutations
W: Two permutations of n items generate a group. Find the shortest nonempty word in them and their inverses, with no immediate cancellations, that multiplies out to the identity. A proposed word is easy to check, so the decision version is in NP when the length bound is written in unary. Is it NP-hard?
M: For $a,b\in S_n$ let $g(a,b)$ be the least length of a nonempty freely reduced word $w$ in $a^{\pm1},b^{\pm1}$ with $w(a,b)=\mathrm{id}$ (the girth of the Cayley graph of $\langle a,b\rangle$ with respect to $\{a^{\pm1},b^{\pm1}\}$). Is $\{(a,b,1^k):g(a,b)\le k\}$ NP-complete? Or can $g(a,b)$ be computed in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,g(a,b))$?

title: The exact constant for Gap-Hamming
W: Alice and Bob each hold an n-bit string and must tell whether the strings differ in noticeably more than half the positions or noticeably fewer, with a gap of g√n. This is known to need order n bits. Find the exact constant in front of n.
M: For $g>0$ let $\mathrm{GHD}_{n,g}$ be the promise problem on $x,y\in\{0,1\}^n$: output 1 if $|x\oplus y|\ge n/2+g\sqrt n$ and 0 if $|x\oplus y|\le n/2-g\sqrt n$. It is known that $R_{1/3}(\mathrm{GHD}_{n,g})=\Theta(n)$. Prove that $c(g)=\lim_n R_{1/3}(\mathrm{GHD}_{n,g})/n$ exists and determine it. In particular, decide whether $c(g)<1$ for all $g$, and find the behaviour of $c(g)$ as $g\to0$ and as $g\to\infty$.

title: Finding a vertex that beats half the field
W: In any round-robin tournament on n players, some player beats at least half of the others. How many match results must you look up to find such a player? Finding a player with the most wins is known to need almost all results. Is order n log n lookups enough here, or are almost all results needed again?
M: Let $Q(n)$ be the deterministic query complexity (queries reveal the orientation of one edge) of the search problem: given a tournament $T$ on $[n]$, output $v$ with $d^+_T(v)\ge(n-1)/2$. Clearly $Q(n)\ge\lceil(n-1)/2\rceil$. Determine $Q(n)$ up to a constant factor. In particular, decide whether $Q(n)=O(n\log n)$ or $Q(n)=\Theta(n^2)$, and determine the randomized complexity.
